newsitem.title: USA: EMI's new catalog business starts operations.
newsitem.headline: EMI's new catalog business starts operations.

text.p: Newly formed EMI-Capitol Entertainment Properties began operations Tuesday, aiming to boost sales by drumming up new ways to sell treasured properties like Beatles music, President Bruce Kirkland said.

The estimated $300 million music catalog company was created by EMI Group Plc's EMI-Capitol Music Group North America as the world's six major record labels are seeing catalog sales fall at the retail level.
"Catalog is a substantial and healthy business, but there is a decline, which has a lot to do with retail," Kirkland said in an interview.
The new company will focus on albums from artists no longer signed to EMI-Capitol, which include landmark titles from its vast vaults like the Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Garth Brooks and Pink Floyd.

Kirkland expects the business to be profitable in the first year. Kirkland, who was a major player behind the Beatles' record-setting "Anthology" series, said joint ventures with large consumer-oriented corporations are key to boosting catalog sales.
"I believe there will be growth at traditional retail channels, but we'll also be looking to exploit other (sales) channels," he said.
For instance, EMI-Capitol Entertainment will seek to promote its catalog albums much like Walt Disney Co. has successfully done by marketing movie videos along with consumer products.
He said Disney ships millions of units by using other companies to leverage its advertising.
"Corporate America understands that music is the way they image their products and sell their products. There are huge opportunities for us to marry music with other strategic products," he said.
Kirkland said catalog sales account for between 35 percent and 40 percent of most big labels' sales. "We would be consistent with that," he said.
Another example of creative marketing would be to create a compilation of old soundtracks and sell them on movie cable channels to a ready-made, movie-loving audience, he said.
"This would be more effective than just putting old soundtracks on retail shelves," Kirkland said.
He denied reports that his move to the new unit reflected a shakeout at the parent company and a fallout with Capitol Records Chief Executive Officer Gary Gersh.
